title: Agricultural Bank v Oshikoto Fruit and Vegetables (HC-MD-CIV-ACT-CON-2021-02543) [2025] NAHCMD 548
text:
REPUBLIC OF NAMIBIA
HIGH COURT OF NAMIBIA MAIN DIVISION, WINDHOEK
JUDGMENT
             Case No.: HC-MD-CIV-ACT-CON-2021/02543
In the matter between:
AGRICULTURAL BANK OF NAMIBIA LTD		                              PLAINTIFF
and
OSHIKOTO FRUIT AND VEGETABLES (PTY) LTD		    FIRST DEFENDANT
CONCORDIA FARMING (PTY) LTD			          SECOND DEFENDANT
MICHAEL NDAPANDULA COLLY IYAMBO                              THIRD DEFENDANT
Neutral citation:	Agricultural Bank of Namibia Ltd v Oshikoto Fruit and Vegetables (Pty) Ltd (HC-MD-CIV-ACT-CON-2021/02543) [2025] NAHCMD 548 (16 September 2025)
Coram:	OBBES AJ
Heard:	27 August 2025
Delivered:	16 September 2025
Flynote:	Summary judgment – Application under High Court Rule 60(1) – Requirements restated — Defendant opposing must disclose material facts constituting a bona fide defence which is good in law. Defence – Alleged compromise/novation – Reliance placed on correspondence – On proper interpretation, correspondence did not evidence or constitute a settlement agreement, compromise, or novation – Defendants failed to establish a triable or arguable issue – Summary judgment granted.
Summary:  The plaintiff applied for summary judgment under High Court Rule 60(1) for amounts due under several loan agreements and related suretyship undertakings. The defendants did not dispute the plaintiff’s cause of action, computation of amounts, or liability at the time action was instituted, but opposed summary judgment on the basis that the matter was allegedly settled through a resolution of the plaintiff’s Board communicated in correspondence, which they contended constituted a compromise and/or novation.
Held that, the opposing affidavit has not established a ‘settlement agreement’ as contended by the defendants.  
Held that, mindful of the principles pertaining to compromise and novation, these have simply not been duly and properly established in the opposing affidavit sufficient for this court to conclude that the defendants have disclosed facts on which they appear to have a defence which is bona fide and good in law.  
Held further that, the defendants have failed to put forward a triable and arguable issue on this score.
Held further that, summary judgment is accordingly granted in favour of the plaintiff against the defendants.
ORDER
Summary judgment in respect of the relief sought in prayer 1 of the notice of application for summary judgment is refused.  
The application for summary judgment (in the respects indicated herein) is granted in favour of the plaintiff in the following terms:
As and against the first defendant:
Payment of the sum of N$2 012 702,72 plus interest at 9 per cent per annum on N$1 230 983 as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment calculated yearly on 30 April and 10.5 per cent per annum on N$781 719,72 as from 31 May 2021 to date of payment calculated on the end of each month and added to the interest-bearing sums.
Payment of the sum of N$2 267 741,66 plus interest at 9 per cent per annum on N$1 356 477,67 as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment calculated yearly on 31 January and 10.5 per cent per annum on N$911 263,99 as from 31 May 2021 to date of payment calculated on the end of each month and added to the interest-bearing sums.
Payment of the sum of N$1 074 837,80 plus interest at 8.75 per cent per annum on N$814 415,89 as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment calculated yearly on 30 April and 10.25 per cent per annum on N$260 421,91 as from 31 May 2021 to date of payment calculated on the end of each month and added to the interest-bearing sums.
Payment of the sum of N$12 433 804,82 plus interest at 8.75 per cent per annum on N$10 038 629,65 as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment calculated yearly on 30 July and 10.25 per cent per annum on N$2 395 175,17 as from 31 May 2021 to date of payment calculated on the end of each month and added to the interest-bearing sums.
Payment of the sum of N$4 241 958,52 plus interest at 9 per cent per annum on N$3 242 498,88 as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment calculated yearly on 31 January and 10.5 per cent per annum on N$911 263,99 as from 31 May 2021 to date of payment calculated on the end of each month and added to the interest-bearing sums.
As and against the second defendant, jointly and severally with the first defendant, the one paying the other to be absolved:
Payment of the sum of N$11 499 740.
Interest on the aforesaid amount at the rate of 9 per cent per annum, in respect of annexures A, B and E and 8.5 per cent per annum, in respect of annexures C and D, respectively, as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment, the total of which is limited to the amount of N$2 299 948.
As and against the third defendant, jointly and severally with the first defendant, the one paying the other to be absolved:
Payment of the sum of N$11 499 740.
Interest on the aforesaid amount at the rate of 9 per cent per annum, in respect of annexures A, B and E and 8.5 per cent per annum, in respect of annexures C and D, respectively, as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment.
The first defendant is ordered to pay costs of suit on an attorney and client scale.
The second and third defendants are ordered to pay costs of suit.
The summary judgment application is finalised and removed from the roll.
JUDGMENT
OBBES AJ:
Introduction
[1]    	This matter concerns an application for summary judgment launched in November 2021 (‘this application’). This application followed the initiation by the plaintiff of an action in July 2021. The description of the parties appears from the pleadings filed of record.
The claim
[2]	From the amended particulars of claim dated 17 September 2021 (‘the amended particulars of claim’), it appears that:
The cause of action in relation to the first defendant relates to five written loan agreements entered into between the plaintiff and the first defendant on or about 12 October 2017, copies of which are annexed to the amended particulars of claim marked annexures A, B, C, D and E.  The plaintiff alleged that the first defendant, in material breach of its repayment obligations towards the plaintiff, failed to pay the instalments as and when same became due and payable and, as of 25 June 2020, was indebted to the plaintiff in the total sum of N$20 188 716.36 (in respect of the loan agreements annexures A, B, C, D and E) of which N$2 562 942.42, excluding further interest and legal costs, was the arrear amount respectively for loan number 10017892 (annexure A), 10017830 (annexure B), 10017831 (annexure C) and 10017832 (annexure D).  
The plaintiff alleged that on 8 November 2017, and as security for the aforementioned indebtedness in the plaintiff’s favour, the first defendant caused a General Notarial Bond to be registered over its immovable property (the said bond formed annexure GN1 to the amended particulars of claim).  
The plaintiff alleged that the first defendant failed to comply with its obligations in terms of the General Notarial Bond and the loan agreements and that the plaintiff is entitled to an order that the General Notarial Bond be perfected.  
The plaintiff alleged that on or about 25 June 2020, the plaintiff and the first defendant concluded a written repayment arrangement agreement (attached to the amended particulars of claim marked annexure F), and in terms whereof the first defendant agreed to repay the amount then in arrears, in the respects indicated in the amended particulars of claim. The plaintiff further alleged that the first defendant agreed to pay the legal costs incurred in the collection of the outstanding balance on a scale as between attorney and client, including collection commission on capital interest and costs, plus further interest as agreed.  
The plaintiff alleged that the first defendant also failed to comply with the terms of the repayment arrangement agreement.  
The plaintiff maintained that as a result of the breach alleged, the full outstanding balance(s) on each of the loan agreements ‘have now become due and payable’.  
The plaintiff proceeded to set out what it alleged the first defendant was and remains indebted to the plaintiff in respect of as at 30 April 2021, and further that despite demand, the first defendant failed and/or neglected to pay the said amounts to the plaintiff despite being due and payable.  
The plaintiff further alleged that on 18 March 2021, the second defendant executed a written deed of surety in favour of the plaintiff (a copy of which was annexed to the amended particulars of claim marked annexure M).  In terms thereof, the second defendant bound itself as surety and co-principal debtor with the first defendant for the due and punctual performance by the first defendant of all its obligations towards the plaintiff for the amount of N$11 499 740 plus interest, charges and costs, and the second defendant renounced the benefits of excussion and division.  Further, it was alleged that the second defendant agreed to register a surety mortgage bond as collateral security over the immovable property described in paragraph 24.3 of the amended particulars of claim. 
The plaintiff alleged that as collateral security for the second defendant’s indebtedness arising from the deed of surety, the second defendant caused to be registered a Surety Mortgage Bond number B1642/2021, for the amount of N$11 499 740 plus an additional amount of N$2 299 948 as preferent charge for costs and other matters inclusive of interest and charges.  The said bond was attached to the amended particulars of claim marked annexure N, and such was registered in favour of the plaintiff over the immovable property of the second defendant described in the amended particulars of claim.  
The plaintiff alleged that in terms of the mortgage bond, the second defendant renounced the benefits of certain legal exceptions (identified in the amended particulars of claim), and accepted full liability as surety and co-principal debtor with the first and second defendants of all obligations towards the plaintiff.  
Further, the plaintiff alleged that on 18 March 2021 and at Windhoek the third defendant executed a written deed of surety in favour of the plaintiff. A copy of that deed of surety was annexed to the amended particulars of claim marked annexure O.  
In terms of that deed of surety, it was alleged, the third defendant bound himself as surety and co-principal debtor with the first defendant for the due and punctual performance by the first defendant of all its obligations towards the plaintiff for the amount of N$11 499 740, plus interest, charges and costs, and renounced the benefits of excussion and division.  
Premised on the aforementioned, the plaintiff alleged that the second and third defendants are therefore liable to the plaintiff in the amount of N$11 499 740 plus interest thereon at the rate of 9 per cent per annum, in respect of annexures A, B and E and 8.5 per cent per annum in respect of annexures C and D respectively, as from 31 May 2021 to date of final payment, plus further charges and costs which amount, in respect of the second defendant only, is limited to the amount of N$2 299 948 only.  
In conclusion, the plaintiff alleged that all of the aforesaid amounts are ‘now due and payable’. In addition, the plaintiff announced that it intended to, simultaneously with judgment, apply for an order that the immovable property referred to in the amended particulars of claim be declared executable.  
The second defendant and any other interested party were stated to be ‘obliged’ and were invited, in the amended particulars of claim, to place facts and submissions before the court to enable the court to consider them when the plaintiff applies for judgment, failing which, it may result in an order declaring the immovable property executable.  
[3]	At the hearing of this application, the plaintiff indicated that it does not persist with seeking summary judgment in respect of the relief sought in prayer 9 of the notice of application for summary judgment, concerning declaring the immovable property executable. This aspect, and the arguments advanced in relation thereto (including concerning the ‘moratorium’ sought to be relied upon by the defendants), are, consequently, not required to be further addressed. The plaintiff’s counsel, furthermore, did not point the court to any authority on the basis of which the relief sought in prayer 1 of the notice of application for summary judgment (an order perfecting a notarial bond) could be sought under High Court Rule 60(1). I am not persuaded that, in the circumstances, the relief sought in prayer 1 is competent in proceedings of this nature. There is, however, authority to the effect that summary judgment may be applied for in respect of any claim falling within the classes recognised in High Court Rule 60(1), even if the summons includes other claims as well. I proceed to consider those claims which, in my view, fall within the classes so recognised.
The grounds of opposition
[4]	The defendants’ ‘opposing/answering affidavit’ (‘the opposing affidavit’) was deposed to in June 2025.
[5]	In the opposing affidavit, the defendants pinned their colours to the mast.  Subject to what is stated below, issue was not taken with the plaintiff’s cause of action or with the basis and computation of the amounts claimed or, for that matter, with the defendants’ liability – at the time the action was initiated – in respect of what the plaintiff claimed. I add that the plaintiff, in its particulars of claim, relied on certain certificates of indebtedness and alleged that ‘a certificate signed by the Chief Executive Officer or by any manager of the Plaintiff showing the actual amount of capital and interest then outstanding, shall be prima facie proof of the First Defendants' indebtedness to the Plaintiff’.
[6]	The centre point of the defendants’ opposition is encapsulated in para 11 of the opposing affidavit:
‘The Defendants aver that following the institution of proceedings by the Plaintiff before this Honorable Court, the parties entered into settlement agreement on or about 9 December 2024, pursuant to which they agreed to a restructuring of the Defendants' loans, a decision which was duly taken by the Plaintiff’.
[7]	The defendants place principal reliance on two annexures to the opposing affidavit: annexure MI2 (being a letter dated 27 February 2024 on the letterhead of Bellatrix Green Finance Facility (Pty) Ltd [‘Bellatrix’] addressed to the Managing Director of Tsinsibis Agriculture (Pty) Ltd [‘Tsinsibis’]) and annexure MI3 (being a letter dated 9 December 2024 on the letterhead of the plaintiff [apparently authored by the Manager: Legal Services] addressed to ‘Bellatrix SME Finance’). 
[8]	According to the defendants, Bellatrix and Tsinsibis were brought in as investors with the view of rescuing ‘their farm from ultimately being sold in execution’.
[9]	The defendants alleged that on 27 February 2024, Bellatrix sent a letter to the plaintiff in which it offered a proposal relating to the restructuring of the defendants’ loans.  
[10]	The defendants alleged that the plaintiff, ‘through its Board’, deliberated on the ‘request by Bellatrix as set out in its letter of 27 February 2024’ and that ‘the Board took a resolution in respect of the said request’ (‘the resolution’). For the latter allegation, the defendants relied on annexure MI3. I quote the pertinent content of annexure MI3 below:
‘Bellatrix SME Finance
Unit 12 Andimba Toivo ya Toivo Street
Southern Industrial Area
Windhoek
Namibia
Dear Mr Kalumbu
Re: Oshikoto Fruit & Veg (Pty) Ltd - Investor proposal requests considerations
1. Your letter dated 27 February 2024 and your subsequent email dated 4th September 2024 bear reference. 
2. We recently concluded our committee and board meetings where your requests to Agribank were tabled.
3. After deliberations, the Board resolved as follows:
i)	The waiving of 100% of the arrears (at the time of submission was N$17,074,481.14) was declined.
ii) 	The grace period of 1 year and 3 months to allow for planting, harvesting, packaging, distribution, and collection of funds from customers was approved.
iii) 	The initial approval of a down payment amount of N$4 million to be reduced to N$2 million as requested was approved, however the remaining N$2 million be added to the loan capital, totaling N$22 million. 
iv) 	In the event that the investor has no sufficient collateral to provide cover for the entire loan capital amount, the loan agreement shall make provision for an automatic cession of funds due to Agribank from the produce sales. 
4. With those conditions, kindly advice if the branch can go ahead with finalizing the loan application submission.
5. In addition, kindly also advice if the grant agreement with the USADF was finally signed off and provide us with a copy of the agreement for purposes of compiling the loan application pack.
Kind regards
_____________
K. Angula
Man: Legal Services’
[11]	The defendants submitted that they ‘duly responded’ to the resolution and ‘authorised’ the plaintiff to proceed with the finalisation and submission of the loan application, in ‘accordance’ with the resolution.  No details were provided on this score in the opposing affidavit.  
[12]	The defendants further maintained that the resolution ‘amounts to settlement agreement between the plaintiff and the defendants’ and that it is a ‘valid agreement of compromise and/or novation which is intended to avoid litigation between the plaintiff and the defendants on the cause of action which became settled’.  
[13]	Further, the defendants alleged that ‘notwithstanding the resolution conveyed to the defendants in the letter dated 9 December 2024’, the plaintiff, without prior consultation with the defendants, ‘unilaterally and purportedly withdrew the approved loan restructuring in the amount of N$22 million or alternatively refused to implement the same and proceeded with legal action against the defendants’.  
[14]	The defendants maintained that the plaintiff is a creature of statute, established in terms of the Agricultural Bank Act 5 of 2003, and stated that it is thus ‘an administrative body’. The defendants submitted that having made a ‘final decision’ in this regard, the plaintiff became functus officio and was thereby precluded from ‘revoking the loan approval previously granted to the defendants’. The defendants alleged that the plaintiff exercises a discretion which must be done fairly, reasonably and in compliance with the requirements of the common law and Art 18 of the Namibian Constitution.  
[15]	The defendants further maintained that the plaintiff seeks to act in terms of a debt that was settled by the parties and seeks to unlawfully execute on immovable property (being the immovable property identified in the amended particulars of claim). The latter aspect, for reasons referred to above, does not require further consideration.
[16]	According to the defendants, the plaintiff has no contractual basis upon which it can approach this court on the same cause of action that was ‘settled by the parties’. 
[17]	In short, it was stated that the plaintiff is bound by the resolution and cannot disregard its decisions and proceed to prosecute its legal proceedings against the defendants based on the original cause of action. 
[18]	The defendants further referred to certain correspondence exchanged between the parties, including a letter dated 4 June 2025 (annexure MI5 to the opposing affidavit), where, according to the defendants, it was ‘admitted that the parties had indeed entered into settlement negotiations.  However, the Plaintiff proceeded to deny that the resolution dated 09 December applied to the Defendants, asserting instead that said resolution pertained to Bellatrix’.  
[19]	The defendants took issue with this and stated that the resolution pertained to the first defendant and that ‘Bellatrix acted as a partner or representative of the defendants during the course of the relevant negotiations’. The defendants did not indicate when, where and how Bellatrix was engaged as ‘a partner or representative’, and no confirmatory affidavit was filed for or on behalf of Bellatrix.  
[20]	The defendants further denied that the resolution was granted subject to any conditions other than those expressly stated therein, and sought to address a stance adopted by the plaintiff in its letter of 4 June 2025 (annexure MI5).  
[21]	In sum, the defendants submitted that they have made out a bona fide defence to the plaintiff’s claim, have ‘clearly set out the material facts relied upon for the defence’, and ultimately sought an order to the effect that this application be dismissed with costs. 
The plaintiff’s submissions
[22]	In the heads of argument filed on behalf of the plaintiff, it was submitted inter alia that:
The defendants admit owing the claim amounts in question and that there is ‘no basis upon which the Court can refuse summary judgment because the defendants have clearly not set out a bona fide defence to the claim’.
Annexure MI2 was addressed by the Managing Director of Bellatrix to the Managing Director of Tsinsibis. The plaintiff submitted that it is common cause that Bellatrix and Tsinsibis are not parties to the loan agreements forming the subject matter of the dispute.  The subject matter of the letter unequivocally stated ‘Conditional Approval : Tsinsibis Agriculture (Pty) Limited’.  
The aforementioned letter is not a proposal letter addressed by Bellatrix to the plaintiff. 
In reference to annexure MI3, it states that ‘with those conditions, kindly advice if the branch can go ahead with finalizing the loan application submission.  In addition, kindly also advice if the grant agreement with USADF was finally signed off and provide us with a copy for purposes of compiling the loan application pack’. The plaintiff placed certain emphasis on the abovementioned quotations.  
Annexure MI3 was preliminary in nature and subject to the conditions contained therein before the loan could be approved.  Annexure MI3 cannot be said to have constituted a final decision.  
Annexure MI11 to the opposing affidavit (being a letter dated 17 June 2025 addressed by Bellatrix ‘SME Finance’ to the plaintiff) reflected that Bellatrix did not ‘go ahead’ with the finalisation of the loan application with the plaintiff.  This conclusion is apparent from the letter addressed by Bellatrix to the plaintiff on 17 June 2025, bearing the subject ‘Proposed Revised Tsinsibis Agriculture (Pty) Limited (Concordia Farm) Funding Structure’.  
It is apparent from annexure MI11 that it is a revised proposal by Bellatrix on terms that are different to those which were conditionally approved by the plaintiff.  
In the circumstances, it is axiomatic that the conditions set out in annexure MI3 were not met by Bellatrix, thus its ‘conditionally approved loan agreement’ with the plaintiff fell away.  
In the circumstances, the point raised by the defendants of functus officio does not arise in this matter.  The plaintiff’s claims arise from a contractual relationship with the defendants (and that relationship is regulated by the terms of the contract), and in any event, the plaintiff’s ‘impugned decision was not final but rather conditional on Bellatrix first satisfying the conditions precedent’.  
Although the plaintiff is a statutory body and derives its powers to enter into contracts with persons engaged in agriculture, or in activities related to agriculture, from statute, it derives its powers to enforce and/or cancel annexure MI3 from the terms contained in annexure MI3 and the common law.
It did not perform an administrative action nor did it exercise a public power and instead the plaintiff acted as a ‘contracting party from a position no different from what it would have been in had it been a private individual or institution’.  On that basis, it was further submitted that the defendants’ reliance on Art 18 and the common law is of no moment or consequence, misplaced and irrelevant.
The defendants’ reliance on a compromise and/or novation is ‘fallacious, bad in law and a desperate attempt to clasp at drifting straws so as to spew a defence solely for the purposes of delay’.  
The defendants appear to have forgotten that the first defendant failed to pay the instalments as of 25 June 2020.  It was further submitted that the claim amount is substantial and continues to accrue interest thereon as the defendants ‘string along the rights of plaintiff to recover its debt from them’.  
This is the approach adopted by the defendants despite admitting in the circumstances that it is liable to the plaintiff for the ‘claim amount’.  
It is clear that the defendants have no case in the action and that they mounted ‘sham defences’ and that, furthermore, they should be prevented from ‘defeating the rights of the plaintiff by occasioning it any further delay which would thereby cause it greater loss whilst it is endeavouring to enforce its rights’.  
The defendants’ submissions
[23]	In the heads of argument filed on behalf of the defendants, it was submitted inter alia that:
The plaintiff compromised on its original cause of action by way of a resolution taken by its Board.
Despite the resolution, the plaintiff denies that the matter has become settled as per the resolution and insists on proceeding with this application. 
The defendants took issue with the plaintiff’s submission that the resolution was preliminary in nature and subject to conditions in annexure MI3 before the loan could be approved. 
The plaintiff took a decision on the offer that was made by the defendants (with Bellatrix as an investor) to it.  It was submitted that nothing in the 9 December 2024 letter (annexure MI3) suggests that such an acceptance was preliminary in nature and conditional.  
Nothing in the resolution is indicative that the approved terms were conditional.  
In reference to the letter of 17 June 2025, it was authored a significant period after the resolution was taken and after the plaintiff had ‘purportedly withdrawn the resolution’ and further that ‘nothing turns on this letter which was prompted by the purported withdrawal of the resolution’.  
Nothing suggests that the resolution was subjected to any future events.  
The plaintiff’s resolution is ‘irrefutable and the suggestion that it was conditional and not final should be rejected’.  
The ‘Board resolution passed on the 9th of December 2024 amounts to a settlement agreement between the plaintiff and the defendants and therefore, it is a valid agreement of compromise and/or novation which is intended to avoid litigation between the plaintiff and the defendants on the cause of action which became settled’.  
The plaintiff has no contractual basis upon which it can proceed with the litigation or this application on the same cause of action that was ‘settled by the parties’.  
A ‘compromise was lawfully struck between the parties, as there was an offer by the defendants and acceptance by the plaintiff (resolution of 9 December 2024) in relation to settling the plaintiff’s claim as set out in the particulars of claim’.  
The plaintiff is a creature of statute and exercises public power in its dealings in terms of the Agricultural Bank of Namibia Act 5 of 2003. Reference was made to Sections 7 and 11 of the said Act. 
Applicable legal principles – summary judgment
[24]	High Court Rule 60(1) allows a plaintiff to apply for summary judgment in certain defined circumstances.  
[25]	High Court Rule 60(5)(b) allows a defendant, in response to an application for summary judgment, to satisfy the court by affidavit that it has a bona fide defence to the action. The rule further provides that the affidavit ‘must disclose fully the nature and grounds of the defence and the material facts relied on’. 
[26]	Pertinent principles concerning a defendant resisting a summary judgment application were recently restated in Marais NO v Shen:
‘[6]	I quote from the locus classicus judgment of Maharaj v Barclays National Bank what the duty of a defendant is in a summary judgment application. Corbett JA says the following:
‘Accordingly, one of the ways in which a defendant may successfully oppose a claim for summary judgment is by satisfying the courts by affidavit that he has a bona fide defense to the claim, where the defense is based upon facts in the sense that material facts alleged by the plaintiff in his summons or combined summons are disputed or new facts are alleged constituting a defense the Court does not attempt to decide these issues or to determine whether or not there is a balance of probabilities in favor of the one party or the other. All that the court inquiries into is a, whether the defendant has fully disclosed the nature and grounds of his defense and the material facts upon which it is founded, and b whether on the facts so disclosed, the defendant appears to have, as to either the whole or part of the claim, a defence which is both bona fide and good in law. If satisfied on these matters, the Court must refuse summary judgment, either wholly or in part, as the case may be.’ 
[27]	In First National Bank of Namibia v Gariseb this court restated the pertinent principles thus:
‘[15]	Summary judgement is regulated by rule 60 of the rules of the High Court. This remedy is available to a plaintiff to obtain judgment summarily without the necessity of going to trial in spite of the fact though an intention to raise a defence has been intimated by the delivery of a notice to intention to defend.
[16]	The legal principles on summary judgment are trite: Sibeya J reiterated in Standard Bank Namibia Limited vs A - Z Investments Holdings (Proprietary) Limited  that summary judgments are drastic remedies available to a plaintiff where no bona fide defence to the claim exists. The court relied on the principles from Kukuri v Social Security Commission as Mainga J discussed the drastic remedy of summary judgments and quoted with approval the following passages by Corbett JA in Maharaj v Barclays National Bank Ltd:
	‘the grant of the remedy is based upon the supposition that the plaintiff’s claim is unimpeachable and that the defendant’s defence is bogus or bad in law.’ 
[17]	Mainga J continued at 426A-E to say the following: 
	‘Accordingly, one of the ways in which the defendant may successfully oppose a claim for summary judgment is by satisfying the Court by affidavit that he has a bona fide defence to the claim. Where the defence is based upon facts, in the sense that material facts alleged by the plaintiff in his summons, or combined summons, are disputed or new facts are alleged constituting a defence, the Court does not attempt to decide these issues or to determine whether or not there is a balance of probabilities in favour of the one party or the other. 
All that the Court enquires into is: 
(a) whether the defendant has fully disclosed the nature and the grounds of his defence and the material facts upon which it is founded, and 
(b) whether on the facts so disclosed the defendant appears to have, as to either the whole or part of the claim, a defence which is bona fide and good in law. 
If satisfied on these matters the Court must refuse summary judgment, either wholly or in part, as the case may be. . . in my view, that, while the defendant need not deal exhaustively with the facts and the evidence relied upon to substantiate them, he must at least disclose his defence and the material facts upon which it is based with sufficient particularity and completeness to enable the Court to decide whether the affidavit discloses a bona fide defence. (See generally, Herb Dyers (Pty) Ltd v Mohamed and Another, 1965 (1) SA 31 (T); Caltex Oil (SA) Ltd v Webb and Another, 1965 (2) SA 914 (N); Arend and Another v Astra Furnishers (Pty) Ltd, supra at pp.303-4; Shepstone v Shepstone, 1974 (2) SA 462 (N). At the same time the defendant is not expected to formulate his opposition to the claim with the precision that would be required of a plea; nor does the court examine it by the standards of pleading. (See Estate Potgieter v Elliot, 1948 (1) SA 1084 (C) at p 1087; Herb Dyers case, supra at p 32.)”’
[18]	Sibeya J further stated that the answering affidavit must disclose the nature of defence and the material facts relied upon. Accordingly, the defendant need not deal exhaustively with the facts and evidence relied upon to substantiate those facts, but he must at least disclose his defence and the material facts upon which it is based with sufficient particularity and completeness to enable the Court to determine whether the affidavit discloses a bona fide defence or not. 
[19]	Furthermore, Geier J stated in Magic Builders Centre (Pty) Ltd v Fysal Fresh Produce  that summary judgment proceedings are not determined with reference to the principles pertaining to the resolution of disputes in motion proceedings – i.e. where the court is to determine the outcome, on a comparison of the affidavits, filed by the parties, with reference to those principles – but merely and mainly – with reference to the content of the defendant’s opposing affidavits – which should disclose a bona fide defence and the material facts relied upon therefore, in order to determine whether or not summary judgment is to be granted or refused. The court further pointed out that the threshold to ward off summary judgment proceedings is very low. Accordingly:
‘What the court enquires into is whether the defendant has put forward a triable and arguable issue in the sense that there is a reasonable possibility that the interpretation contended for by the defendant may succeed at trial, and, if successful, will establish a defence that is good in law.  Similarly, where the defendant relies upon a point of law, the point raised must be arguable and establish a defence that is good in law. (footnotes omitted)’
[20]	What the court needs to determine therefore is what is contained in the opposing affidavit: whether the defendant discloses his defence and the material facts upon which it is based with sufficient particularity and completeness to enable the Court to determine whether the affidavit discloses a bona fide defence or not. The defence disclosed must be a triable issue or a point of law that is arguable and that will establish a defence that is good in law. The converse is true as set out in Breitenbach v Fiat SA (EDMS) BPK, that ‘All that is required is that the defendant’s defence be not set out so baldly, vaguely or laconically that the court, with due regard to all the circumstances, receives the impression that the defendant has, or may have dishonestly sought to avoid the dangers inherent in the presentation of a fuller or clearer version of the defence which he claims to have.’ 
[28]	In Kukuri v Social Security Commission, the Supreme Court held that:
‘Where the statements of fact are equivocal or ambiguous or contradictory or fail to canvass matters essential to the defence raised, then the affidavit does not comply with the Rule.  See Arend and Another v Astra Furnishers (Pty) Ltd 1974 (1) SA 298 (C) at 304A-B’.
[29]	Thus, in applications of this kind, the court’s function includes inquiring into whether the defendants have fully disclosed the nature and grounds of their defence and the material facts upon which it is founded, and whether, on the facts so disclosed, the defendants appear to have a defence which is both bona fide and good in law.   On the latter aspect, this court is to consider whether the defendants have put forward a triable and arguable issue.
Consideration
[30]	The defendants’ characterisation of annexure MI2 as a letter sent by Bellatrix to the plaintiff in ‘which it offered a proposal relating to restructuring of the defendants’ loans’ is not borne out. 
[31]	On the face of it, annexure MI2 was addressed by Bellatrix to Tsinsibis, and referred to ‘your application’ (suggesting an application by Tsinsibis).  
[32]	Ex facie annexure MI2, while it appears to concern a ‘non-binding offer’ relating to the restructuring of ‘AGRIBANK’s loan’, it was not addressed to the plaintiff.  
[33]	Annexure MI2 does not support the allegation made in the opposing affidavit that on ‘27 February 2024 Bellatrix Pty Ltd sent a letter to Agribank on which it offered a proposal relating to restructuring of the Defendants' loans’.
[34]	The defendants’ stance is that the plaintiff’s Board ‘deliberated on the request by Bellatrix as set out in its letter …’. However, annexure MI2 contains no such request.  Instead, in its text, it states inter alia that ‘we are pleased to inform you that your application was favorably considered by our Investment Committee for the Green Finance Facility of N$6 000 000 …’. 
[35]	In context, it is not apparent on what basis the opposing affidavit can maintain that the plaintiff’s Board ‘took a resolution in respect of the said request’.
[36]	The defendants submitted in the opposing affidavit that the ‘resolution passed on the 9th December 2024 amounts to settlement agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendants’. 
[37]	The opposing affidavit, without including necessary particularity, further submits that the defendants ‘duly responded to the above resolution and authorized the Plaintiff to proceed with the finalization and submission of the loan application…’.  Submissions are not statements of fact, and in any event, what the defendants put up on this score is equivocal.  
[38]	The defendants failed to canvass matters essential to the defence sought to be raised.
[39]	Quite apart from that, the defendants themselves seem to recognise that the process involved the submission of a ‘loan application’. This, in itself, illustrates that the resolution was not the final word, so to speak, in relation to what was referred to therein.
[40]	Annexure MI3 appears to indicate terms (or conditions) on which a ‘loan application submission’ could be finalised. It does not, on the papers before me, constitute or evidence a ‘compromise and/or novation’. 
[41]	Novation entails ‘replacing an existing obligation by a new one, the existing obligation being thereby discharged’.  And further:
‘Now 'novation is essentially a question or intention: when parties novate they intend to replace a valid contract by another valid contract'; see the judgment of my Brother BEYERS, relying on a passage from Wessels Law of Contract, in Acacia Mines Ltd v Boshoff, 1958 (4) SA 330 (AD) at p. 337. In the present case there is no evidence that the parties expressly agreed to replace the W/34 contract by the W/64 series. If therefore a novation took place, it can only be inferred. In Electric Process Engraving and Stereo Co v Irwin, 1940 AD 220, CENTLIVRES, J.A., giving the judgment of the Court, said at pp. 226 - 7:
'The law on the subject was clearly enunciated as far back as 1880 in the well-known case of Ewers v The Resident Magistrate of Oudtshoorn and Another, Foord 32, where DE VILLIERS, C.J., said: 'The result of the authorities is that the question is one of intention and that, in the absence of any express declaration of the parties, the intention to effect a novation cannot be held to exist except by way of necessary inference from all the circumstances of the case.'' ’
[42]	A compromise is an ‘agreement between the parties to prevent or terminate a dispute by adjusting their differences by mutual consent. It is trite that a compromise gives rise to new contractual rights and obligations which exist independently of the original cause of action. Once a compromise is reached, the parties are precluded from proceeding on the original cause of action (unless, of course, the compromise provides otherwise)’.  And further:
‘Compromise, or transactio, is the settlement by agreement of disputed obligations, whether contractual or otherwise. If an offer to settle in particular terms is not accepted, the offeree cannot treat an inseparable part of the offer as an acknowledgment of debt and sue on it. Even a criminal charge may be settled by the process known as plea bargaining, and the resulting compromise agreement will be enforceable. If there is no dispute, there can be no compromise. It is a form of novation differing from ordinary novation in that the obligations novated by the compromise must previously have been disputed or uncertain, the essence of compromise being the final settlement of the dispute or uncertainty. Unlike novation, a compromise is binding on the parties even though the original contract was invalid or even illegal, unless the compromise is, on its terms, not enforceable. However the contract may be described by the parties, the court will look at the substance rather than the form in order to decide whether a particular obligation or dispute has been compromised. The onus is on the party alleging that a compromise has been effected, and because compromise is a form of novation and involves the waiver of existing rights (or claimed rights) it must be as clearly and unambiguously proved as any other waiver or novation.’ 
[43]	In my considered view, the opposing affidavit has not established a ‘settlement agreement’ as contended by the defendants. Mindful of the principles pertaining to compromise and novation, these have simply not been duly and properly established in the opposing affidavit sufficient for this court to conclude that the defendants have disclosed facts on which they appear to have a defence which is bona fide and good in law.  The defendants have failed to put forward a triable and arguable issue on this score.
[44]	In the text Herbstein and Van Winsen, The Civil Practice of the High Courts and the Supreme Court of Appeal of South Africa, Fifth Edition (Cilliers et al), at 531, the learned authors opine (in reference to authorities referred to on that page) that the ‘defendant must place on affidavit enough of his evidence to convince the court that the necessary testimony is available to him and that, if it is accepted, it will constitute a defence’. This the defendants failed to do.
[45]	The defendants maintained that the plaintiff is a creature of statute (established in terms of the Agricultural Bank Act 5 of 2003) and is thus an ‘administrative body’.  The defendants submitted that ‘having made a final decision in this regard’, the plaintiff became functus officio and was ‘precluded from revoking the loan approval previously granted to the defendants’.  One need not enter the discussion concerning (a) whether the resolution constitutes administrative action and (b) the issue of functus officio, since the defendants failed to establish a ‘loan approval’ (in respect of the defendants) in the opposing affidavit and given my findings above.
